headline: High-risk shared-state and tool-chain interaction: open-webui can ingest and act on LangGraph outputs, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph can expose application-defined files, stdin/stdout, browsers, and developer-defined tools, while open-webui supports MCP, OpenAPI tools, plugins, and browser-backed workflows. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled content from one side can be reinterpreted as instructions by the other. The interaction is documented by profiles, though not sandboxed.
conditions: IF LangGraph nodes write untrusted content into files or stdout that open-webui later ingests
IF open-webui is configured with MCP/OpenAPI tools that parse model-visible content as instructions
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of LangGraph outputs into open-webui prompts
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent messages
Restrict open-webui tool execution to allowlisted commands
Use a separate workspace directory per agent
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: LangGraph handles model provider API keys and application graph state, and open-webui touches prompts, documents, files, persistent memory, and API keys. Because both have broad network egress and file access, sensitive data can flow from LangGraph-managed state into open-webui storage or outbound calls. The pairwise leakage path is credible from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF LangGraph graph state contains secrets or sensitive documents
IF open-webui persists imported files, chat history, or memory from LangGraph outputs
mitigations: Keep secrets out of LangGraph graph state
Disable open-webui persistence for imported artifacts
Separate API keys per agent and per environment
Restrict outbound connectors in open-webui
requires-engineering: implement field-level redaction before handoff

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write or mutate shared resources: LangGraph can write application-defined files and spawn subprocesses, while open-webui can access local files, mounted volumes, and broad networked tool servers. With shared state and no locking guarantees across the pair, concurrent writes or tool actions can collide and corrupt artifacts or sessions.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, mounted volume, or session-backed resource
IF either agent performs writes without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories and volumes
Serialize writes through one coordinator
Disable concurrent edits to shared artifacts
Use file locks or transactional updates
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is an orchestration layer whose outputs can become downstream inputs, and open-webui is a UI/tooling layer that can act on those outputs via plugins, MCP, or OpenAPI tools. If open-webui treats LangGraph-produced text as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into user-visible actions or tool calls without verification.
conditions: IF open-webui forwards LangGraph output into tool calls or user-facing actions without verification
IF LangGraph emits unverified facts that open-webui renders as authoritative
mitigations: Insert a human review step before actions
Require citations for any forwarded claims
Mark LangGraph output as untrusted in open-webui
Disable auto-execution of tool suggestions
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: LangGraph is open-source library infrastructure with application-defined state, while open-webui stores prompts, documents, notes, calendar events, files, and analytics and can connect to third-party APIs. The profiles show a likely retention/residency mismatch risk for the same data classes, but no direct jurisdictional conflict is documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in open-webui persistence while LangGraph application state retains the same records
IF the deployment relies on different retention or export policies across the two systems
mitigations: Classify data before sharing between agents
Disable analytics for regulated workloads
Align retention settings across both systems
Document deletion/export handling for shared records
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing
